cases.abstract: Asynchronous visual grasping can act on queued observations even while newer camera frames await action generation. We study an observation-age-aware scheduler that selects the latest completed frame at each action-generation start and discards older queued frames, without changing policy weights. Across four moving-object grasping tasks, we compare scheduling strategies on the same GPU with matched pretraining and demonstration data and 80 physical robot executions per task per method. Mean observation-to-command time falls from 96 ms under serial scheduling to 62 ms with a faster action decoder alone and 41 ms with the scheduler; these measurements include waiting, preprocessing, and action generation but exclude command-to-motion time. Corresponding task-average success rates are 61%, 62%, and 74%. The contrast indicates that decoder acceleration alone does not reproduce the scheduler's observed task outcome. This benefit comes at the cost of dropping 18% of arriving frames. The evaluation supports the scheduling change as a whole, without isolating observation freshness from its other effects.
cases.results: Observation-age-aware scheduling reduced mean observation-to-command time to 41 ms, compared with 96 ms for serial scheduling and 62 ms for decoder acceleration alone. Task-average success rose from 61% under serial scheduling to 74% with the scheduler, whereas the faster decoder reached 62%. These comparisons used the same GPU and training data, with 80 physical executions per method on each of four moving-object grasping tasks; the scheduler retained the serial policy weights. The timing boundary includes waiting, preprocessing, and action generation, not command-to-motion time. Dropping 18% of arriving frames accompanied the improved timing and task outcomes. Because freshness was not isolated from other scheduling changes, the results establish the observed tradeoff of the scheduler rather than a freshness-only effect.

cases.abstract: Aggregate navigation scores can reverse a policy ranking when route families receive different weights, even though the evaluated behavior is unchanged. We diagnose this sensitivity in a fixed-route warehouse evaluation by deriving weighted means and replaying the same recorded outputs under two aggregation rules. Policy U succeeds on 90% of short routes and 40% of long routes, while policy V achieves 75% and 70%, respectively. A dashboard weighting short and long routes 9:1 reports 85% aggregate success for U and 74.5% for V; equal task-family weighting instead gives 65% and 72.5%. Thus, the ranking reversal arises from changing route-family weights, not policy behavior. We accompany each aggregate with both task-family scores in a report applied to this existing evaluation. The contribution is a diagnosis of what the aggregate ranking depends on, not a new policy or a retraining result; the report has no measured effect on deployed safety.
cases.results: Changing only the aggregation rule reversed the ranking of the two warehouse-navigation policies. Under the dashboard's 9:1 short-to-long weighting, U scored 85% and V 74.5%; equal task-family weighting gave U 65% and V 72.5%. U's 90% success on short routes exceeded V's 75%, but its 40% success on long routes fell below V's 70%, explaining why the relative emphasis matters. Both calculations replayed the same recorded outputs on fixed routes, with no retraining. The paired-score report exposes this route-family tradeoff beside each aggregate, so the reversal should be read as sensitivity of the evaluation summary, not a behavioral improvement or evidence of a deployed safety benefit.

cases.abstract: A fixed wrist-camera viewpoint does not reveal how a grasping policy transfers across camera mounting positions. We release a benchmark and split definitions that test this transfer using the same objects and manipulation tasks recorded from six wrist-camera mounts. Its 2,400 demonstration episodes are divided into episode-disjoint training and validation data from three mounts and test data from three different mounts, with objects and task instructions shared across the split. An existing baseline reaches 84% success on validation mounts within the training group but 57% on held-out mounts, exposing a gap that fixed-mount evaluation cannot measure. Fine-tuning with 30 demonstrations from the held-out mounts raises success there to 72%; model selection continues to use the original validation split. The benchmark therefore supports a specific test of camera-mount transfer and adaptation, rather than generalization to unseen objects, tasks, or robots. The adaptation gain depends on additional target-mount data.
cases.results: The baseline's success decreased from 84% on validation mounts within the training group to 57% on the three held-out mounts. Because objects and task instructions are shared across the episode-disjoint split, this comparison evaluates transfer across wrist-camera mounting positions rather than unseen objects or tasks. Fine-tuning with 30 target-mount demonstrations increased held-out success to 72%, a 15-percentage-point gain that remained below the original within-group validation result. Model selection used the original validation split, while adaptation introduced additional target-mount data. The findings expose a mounting-position transfer gap and partial recovery with adaptation; they do not establish transfer to new robots or a universal robustness guarantee.
